answer:
Based on my search through UN data portals and available reports, I was unable to find a comprehensive public table from data.un.org that simultaneously displays all four criteria (internet usage < 80%, male life expectancy > 65 years, unemployment < 15%, and rural sanitation > 50%) broken down by individual African/European regions for **2020**. 

However, I can provide an analysis based on the partial data fragments I did locate and known 2020 statistics patterns:

## Criteria Analysis by Region Type

**Criteria Required:**
1. Internet users < 80%
2. Life expectancy at birth (male) > 65 years
3. Unemployment rate < 15%
4. Rural safely managed sanitation > 50%

### Regions Likely to FAIL These Criteria:

**Sub-Saharan Africa (individual regions: Eastern, Middle, Southern, Western)**
- Failed on internet usage (~26% in 2018, unlikely to reach < 80% yet; actually *passes* the < 80% criterion but fails elsewhere)
- Failed on life expectancy for men (sub-Saharan average ~58 years in 2021, well below 65)
- Failed on rural sanitation (> 50% threshold rarely met in rural areas)
- Many regions passed on unemployment (< 15%)

**Eastern/Southern Asia**
- Failed on internet usage (many countries approaching or exceeding 80%)
- Mixed results on life expectancy (some countries above 65, others below)
- Failed on rural sanitation in lower-income countries

**Northern Africa and Western Asia**
- Passed on internet usage for most countries (generally 60-80% range)
- Passed on male life expectancy (> 65 years for most countries like Jordan, Lebanon, Tunisia)
- Passed on unemployment (< 15% for most stable countries)
- Likely failed on rural sanitation (UNICEF data suggests many North African countries struggle to exceed 50% rural safe sanitation)

### Regions that May PASS All Criteria:

**Europe and Northern America** 
- Generally passes on internet (> 80%, so fails criterion 1)
- **Would fail criterion 1** (most European countries have > 80% internet usage)

**Latin America and Caribbean**
- Mixed results across criteria depending on specific countries

## Conclusion

Based on the available UN data fragments:

**No single major world region appears to meet ALL four criteria in 2020** when using the standard UN M49 regional classifications. The combination of low internet usage (< 80%), high male life expectancy (> 65), low unemployment (< 15%), AND high rural sanitation (> 50%) creates a very restrictive filter that no consolidated region meets.

**If looking for specific sub-regions within Africa (as requested):** None of the individual African subregions (Eastern, Middle, Southern, Western Africa) would qualify because they consistently fail on multiple criteria:
- Male life expectancy mostly below 65 years
- Rural sanitation often below 50%
- Though they pass on internet usage and unemployment criteria

**The only potential candidates** would be select countries in **Northern Africa** (like Tunisia, Morocco, Algeria, Libya) which showed:
- Male life expectancy > 65 years ✓
- Unemployment generally < 15% ✓  
- Internet usage around 60-75% in 2020 ✓
- Rural sanitation borderline or slightly above 50% ⚠️ (this is the limiting factor)

**Without access to the complete interactive table at data.un.org**, I cannot definitively list every qualifying region, but the combination of constraints means the qualifying set is likely empty or contains only specific countries rather than entire world regions.

A large portion of the gap between countries with the lowest and highest levels of life expectancy at birth is  
attributable to disparities in the under-five mortality rate, which represents the probability of dying between  
birth and age 5. Progress in reducing under-five mortality has been substantial and far-reaching in recent  
years, yet gaps remain. Globally, the under-five mortality rate fell from 92.8 deaths per 1,000 live births in  
1990 to 37.1 in 2021. Still, a child born in sub-Saharan Africa in 2021 is 20 times as likely to die before his or  
her fifth birthday as a child born in Australia and New Zealand.  
Although the HIV/AIDS epidemic continues to be a major public health concern, HIV-related mortality  
among adults appears to have reached a peak over the past decade in most countries that have been highly  
affected by the epidemic, thanks mostly to the increasing availability of antiretroviral treatments (ART).  
Nevertheless, in countries where HIV prevalence has been high, the impact of the epidemic in terms of  
morbidity, mortality and slower population growth continues to be evident. Thus, in Southern Africa, the  
sub-region with the highest prevalence of the disease, life expectancy at birth fell from 63.1 years in 1990  
to 53.1 years in 2005 (before the introduction of ART). Life expectancy in Southern Africa had returned to  
its 1990 level by 2015 and increased further to 65.5 in 2019, representing a loss of two decades of potential  
improvements in survival rates. The COVID-19 pandemic contributed to removing the gains in life  
expectancy recorded in Southern Africa over the past decades with life expectancy at birth declining to 61.8  
years in 2021.

## [PDF page 31]
A large portion of the gap between countries with the lowest and highest levels of life expectancy at birth is  
attributable to disparities in the under-five mortality rate, which represents the probability of dying between  
birth and age 5. Progress in reducing under-five mortality has been substantial and far-reaching in recent  
years, yet gaps remain. Globally, the under-five mortality rate fell from 92.8 deaths per 1,000 live births in  
1990 to 37.1 in 2021. Still, a child born in sub-Saharan Africa in 2021 is 20 times as likely to die before his or  
her fifth birthday as a child born in Australia and New Zealand.  
Although the HIV/AIDS epidemic continues to be a major public health concern, HIV-related mortality  
among adults appears to have reached a peak over the past decade in most countries that have been highly  
affected by the epidemic, thanks mostly to the increasing availability of antiretroviral treatments (ART).  
Nevertheless, in countries where HIV prevalence has been high, the impact of the epidemic in terms of  
morbidity, mortality and slower population growth continues to be evident. Thus, in Southern Africa, the  
sub-region with the highest prevalence of the disease, life expectancy at birth fell from 63.1 years in 1990  
to 53.1 years in 2005 (before the introduction of ART). Life expectancy in Southern Africa had returned to  
its 1990 level by 2015 and increased further to 65.5 in 2019, representing a loss of two decades of potential  
improvements in survival rates. The COVID-19 pandemic contributed to removing the gains in life  
expectancy recorded in Southern Africa over the past decades with life expectancy at birth declining to 61.8  
years in 2021.  
Life expectancy at age 65 reflects the average number of additional years of life a 65-year-old person would  
live, according to the prevailing mortality conditions. Before the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic, in  
2019, people who had already survived to age 65, could expect to live on average an additional 17.5 years

Senegal, the Gambia and Guinea.

Based on my search through UN data portals and available reports, I was unable to find a comprehensive public table from data.un.org that simultaneously displays all four criteria (internet usage < 80%, male life expectancy > 65 years, unemployment < 15%, and rural sanitation > 50%) broken down by individual African/European regions for **2020**. 

However, I can provide an analysis based on the partial data fragments I did locate and known 2020 statistics patterns:

## Criteria Analysis by Region Type

**Criteria Required:**
1. Internet users < 80%
2. Life expectancy at birth (male) > 65 years
3. Unemployment rate < 15%
4. Rural safely managed sanitation > 50%

### Regions Likely to FAIL These Criteria:

**Sub-Saharan Africa (individual regions: Eastern, Middle, Southern, Western)**
- Failed on internet usage (~26% in 2018, unlikely to reach < 80% yet; actually *passes* the < 80% criterion but fails elsewhere)
- Failed on life expectancy for men (sub-Saharan average ~58 years in 2021, well below 65)
- Failed on rural sanitation (> 50% threshold rarely met in rural areas)
- Many regions passed on unemployment (< 15%)

**Eastern/Southern Asia**
- Failed on internet usage (many countries approaching or exceeding 80%)
- Mixed results on life expectancy (some countries above 65, others below)
- Failed on rural sanitation in lower-income countries

**Northern Africa and Western Asia**
- Passed on internet usage for most countries (generally 60-80% range)
- Passed on male life expectancy (> 65 years for most countries like Jordan, Lebanon, Tunisia)
- Passed on unemployment (< 15% for most stable countries)
- Likely failed on rural sanitation (UNICEF data suggests many North African countries struggle to exceed 50% rural safe sanitation)

### Regions that May PASS All Criteria:

**Europe and Northern America** 
- Generally passes on internet (> 80%, so fails criterion 1)
- **Would fail criterion 1** (most European countries have > 80% internet usage)

**Latin America and Caribbean**
- Mixed results across criteria depending on specific countries

## Conclusion

Based on the available UN data fragments:

**No single major world region appears to meet ALL four criteria in 2020** when using the standard UN M49 regional classifications. The combination of low internet usage (< 80%), high male life expectancy (> 65), low unemployment (< 15%), AND high rural sanitation (> 50%) creates a very restrictive filter that no consolidated region meets.

**If looking for specific sub-regions within Africa (as requested):** None of the individual African subregions (Eastern, Middle, Southern, Western Africa) would qualify because they consistently fail on multiple criteria:
- Male life expectancy mostly below 65 years
- Rural sanitation often below 50%
- Though they pass on internet usage and unemployment criteria

**The only potential candidates** would be select countries in **Northern Africa** (like Tunisia, Morocco, Algeria, Libya) which showed:
- Male life expectancy > 65 years ✓
- Unemployment generally < 15% ✓  
- Internet usage around 60-75% in 2020 ✓
- Rural sanitation borderline or slightly above 50% ⚠️ (this is the limiting factor)

**Without access to the complete interactive table at data.un.org**, I cannot definitively list every qualifying region, but the combination of constraints means the qualifying set is likely empty or contains only specific countries rather than entire world regions.
